paths.title: External application users
paths.when: Use a user pool when application sign-in and supported identity federation fit the product.

flow.title: User / external IdP
flow.detail: Customers; optional Entra ID, Okta, OIDC or SAML federation

flow.title: Cognito user pool
flow.out: ID token → client; access token → API

flow.title: Application / API
flow.detail: Validates signature, issuer, client/audience, expiry and token use

flow.title: App authorization
flow.detail: Code or Verified Permissions decides; application enforces

paths.control: Configure the app client, trusted external IdPs, redirects and API token validation before accepting sign-ins.
paths.credential: User-pool JWTs: ID token for the client sign-in; access token for the configured API. Neither is an AWS access key.
checks: An employee can also be an application user. Their corporate IdP can federate into Cognito; caller category alone does not forbid Cognito.
Need direct access to AWS APIs? A configured Cognito identity pool can exchange supported identity tokens for temporary IAM-role credentials; then use SigV4.
The backend often uses its own workload role for AWS calls. Its S3 permission does not decide which document the end user may read.

alternative.title: Cognito identity pool
alternative.detail: Maps identity to a configured IAM role

alternative.title: Client SDK role session
alternative.detail: Uses expiring access keys and session token

alternative.title: AWS API
alternative.detail: IAM role/resource policies constrain direct access

paths.title: Employees accessing AWS
paths.when: Use Identity Center for centrally assigned workforce SSO and AWS account access.

flow.title: Corporate IdP
flow.detail: Entra ID, Okta, or a supported AD/federation setup

flow.title: Account role session
flow.detail: Permission set provisions the IAM role/policies

flow.title: AWS account / API
flow.detail: Applicable IAM policies and guardrails decide access

paths.control: Configure SAML trust and provision users/groups (SCIM or supported provisioning). Assign permission sets to accounts separately.
paths.credential: Portal/CLI sign-in enables an assigned account role session. AWS API calls use temporary credentials; SAML assertions are not S3 bearer tokens.
checks: SAML handles federation; SCIM handles user/group provisioning. Provisioning alone is not sign-in.
A permission set templates IAM policies for account roles. It does not implement document-level rules in your custom assistant.
Active Directory needs a supported directory integration or federation service; a raw AD password is not an OIDC token.

paths.title: External workload identity
paths.principal: Machine outside the AWS-native role delivery path
paths.target: AWS APIs through an assumed IAM role
paths.when: Use supported OIDC federation when a workload can obtain an assertion from an explicitly trusted issuer.

flow.title: AWS STS + role trust
flow.out: Access key ID + secret + session token

paths.control: Create the IAM OIDC provider and a role trust policy scoped to the intended audience and subject, such as repository/branch or service account.
paths.credential: The JWT is the federation assertion. STS returns temporary AWS credentials with an expiration; the SDK uses them to sign requests.
checks: Gate 1: may this principal assume this role? Gate 2: may that role session perform this resource action? Passing the first does not pass the second.
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the OIDC/web-identity operation. Direct IAM SAML federation uses AssumeRoleWithSAML.
Kubernetes federation depends on the deployment. EKS Pod Identity uses a different native credential path; not every pod uses web-identity federation.

paths.title: AWS-native workloads
paths.target: AWS APIs using its workload role
paths.when: Use service-integrated role credentials instead of shipping long-lived keys to the workload.

flow.title: AWS workload
flow.detail: Lambda, EC2 instance, or ECS task

flow.title: Trusted IAM role
flow.detail: Execution role, instance profile role, or task role

flow.title: SDK credential chain
flow.detail: Retrieves provided credentials; SDK handles signing

flow.title: AWS API
flow.detail: Authorizes role session, action, resource and context

paths.control: Configure the service trust policy and attach the correct execution role, EC2 instance profile, or ECS task role. Grant only required permissions.
paths.credential: Temporary role credentials, not an end-user JWT. Let supported SDK credential providers obtain and refresh them.
checks: The ECS task role is for application calls; the task execution role supports tasks such as pulling images and delivering logs.
A role is a permission-bearing identity, not a permanent access key. Trust allows assumption; permissions govern resulting actions.

paths.title: Enterprise application authorization
paths.principal: Already authenticated application user or agent
paths.when: Use application policy, optionally Verified Permissions, when access depends on business entities and context.

flow.title: Application / API
flow.detail: Derives tenant and trusted resource context

flow.title: App enforcement
flow.detail: Stops denied calls; applies permitted scope

flow.title: Document / action
flow.detail: Retrieval and action APIs enforce the scope

paths.control: Define the Cedar schema/policies, trusted identity source and resource attributes. Keep AWS role permissions and application policies distinct.
paths.credential: A principal/action/resource/context request, or supported identity-source token via IsAuthorizedWithToken. An ALLOW is a decision, not AWS credentials.
checks: Verified Permissions does not perform user sign-in. Its token-based APIs can validate supported identity-source tokens while evaluating policy.
The application is the policy enforcement point: deny on failed authorization and prevent direct retrieval or tool paths that bypass it.
RAG must enforce tenant/document scope before context assembly. A backend IAM role that can query the KB does not imply every user may see every chunk.

paths.title: AI agents
paths.principal: Caller, agent workload, and downstream user delegation
paths.when: Use AgentCore identity capabilities to connect supported inbound authentication and outbound credential needs.

flow.title: Caller / IdP
flow.detail: Supported IdP authenticates user or machine

flow.title: Runtime / Gateway
flow.detail: Configured inbound authorizer checks trust and claims

flow.title: Agent tool client
flow.out: OAuth access token / API key / AWS SigV4

flow.title: Downstream API
flow.detail: Enforces scope, tenant and business rules

paths.control: Configure inbound JWT discovery/claims or IAM permissions, outbound credential providers, workload access and any user consent required by the flow.
paths.credential: Inbound caller tokens and outbound tool credentials are distinct. OAuth user delegation may require consent; AWS targets can use authorized IAM credentials.
checks: Inbound authentication at Runtime/Gateway and outbound credential brokerage have separate configurations. Do not assume the incoming JWT is valid for every tool.
AgentCore Identity does not make every proposed action permissible. Target scopes, Gateway Policy where configured, and business authorization still apply.

protocols.title: JWT
protocols.subtitle: A token format
protocols.purpose: A compact claims container, often signed. The protocol and token profile define how it is used.

flow.title: Token holder
flow.detail: Carries the token to its intended recipient

flow.title: Recipient
flow.detail: Checks signature, issuer, intended recipient and lifetime

points: Common claims: iss = issuer; sub = subject; aud = intended audience; exp = expiry. Requirements depend on the token profile.
Signature validation detects tampering and authenticates the trusted signer. Decoding base64url is not validation; a signed JWT is not necessarily encrypted.
JWT is not an authentication protocol. An OAuth access token can be JWT-shaped or opaque.

protocols.title: OAuth 2.0
protocols.subtitle: Delegated authorization
protocols.purpose: Obtain limited access to a protected resource. This example uses the authorization-code flow with PKCE.
points: The code is exchanged at the token endpoint; it is not the access token. Other grants, such as client credentials, serve different principals.
OAuth alone does not standardize a user login result for the application. ID tokens come from OIDC.

protocols.title: OIDC
protocols.subtitle: Authentication on OAuth 2.0
protocols.purpose: Add a standardized user identity result to an OAuth flow by requesting the openid scope.

flow.title: Application
flow.detail: Validates ID token; creates login session

flow.title: Protected API
flow.detail: Validates its token contract and policy

points: An ID token tells the client about the authentication. Its audience identifies the client; it is not a general-purpose API access token.
The API applies its configured access-token contract. Validate issuer, intended audience/client, expiry, signature and token type as required.
Some integrations explicitly accept ID tokens. Follow that integration's documented contract; do not substitute token types merely because both are JWTs.

protocols.title: SAML 2.0
protocols.subtitle: Enterprise federation
protocols.purpose: Exchange an XML assertion between an explicitly trusted identity provider and a service provider.

flow.title: IAM Identity Center
flow.detail: Validates SAML trust; creates workforce session

points: Metadata/certificates establish the trust relationship. Validate signature, issuer, recipient/audience and validity under the integration contract.
SAML is not a JWT. SCIM provisions users/groups; it is separate from the SAML sign-in. Direct IAM SAML federation can use AssumeRoleWithSAML.

protocols.title: AWS STS
protocols.subtitle: Temporary AWS credentials
protocols.purpose: A trusted federation assertion can be exchanged for an authorized role session. STS is an AWS service, not a login protocol.

flow.title: AWS STS + role trust
flow.out: Access key ID + secret + session token

points: For web identity, call AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. AWS validates the token/provider and role trust conditions before issuing credentials.
The result contains access key ID, secret access key, session token and expiration. SDKs generally sign AWS requests with SigV4.
Authentication tokens do not automatically grant IAM permissions. The role/session and applicable resource policies, boundaries and SCPs still constrain actions.

chunking.title: Default
chunking.note: The service decides the grouping; do not assume sentence preservation also keeps every rule and exception together.

chunking.title: Fixed-size
chunking.purpose: Set token size and overlap explicitly.
chunking.note: The highlighted repeated token IDs are the same content in adjacent chunks. Token labels here are schematic, not a model tokenizer.

chunking.title: Semantic
chunking.purpose: Split around meaning or topic changes.
chunking.note: Semantic splits can still separate a rule from a distant exception. They do not guarantee preservation of document hierarchy.

chunking.title: Hierarchical
chunking.purpose: Retrieve small child matches; return broader parent context.
chunking.note: The parent encloses the child content. Standard hierarchical KB retrieval can substitute parents and collapse several child hits into fewer results; GraphRAG has a different contract.

chunking.title: Custom
chunking.purpose: Use a Lambda transformation for domain boundaries and metadata.
chunking.note: For custom chunking, use the supported no-chunking configuration and Lambda/intermediate-S3 contract. Managed embedding/indexing can remain in place.

security.title: AWS Artifact
security.question: AWS compliance evidence
security.copy: Retrieve AWS reports, certifications and agreements on demand.
security.caveat: Not a continuous infrastructure auditing engine.

security.title: AWS Audit Manager
security.question: Framework audit evidence
security.copy: Continuously collect supported evidence from configured sources for selected framework controls, such as supported ISO 27001 controls; add manual evidence where needed.
security.caveat: Collection frequency varies by source. Evidence is not certification; existing-account/Region availability applies.

security.title: AWS Config
security.question: Resource configuration compliance
security.copy: Record supported resource configurations/history; evaluate configured rules.
security.caveat: A compliant rule result does not establish all application or framework obligations.

security.title: AWS CloudTrail
security.question: API activity auditing
security.copy: Record supported AWS API activity and account events for investigation.
security.caveat: Enable needed event coverage, especially data events; not a prompt-content log.

security.title: Amazon Inspector
security.question: Vulnerability management
security.copy: Continually assess supported EC2, ECR and Lambda workloads for applicable vulnerabilities/exposure.
security.caveat: Supported scan types and resource eligibility differ; it does not scan all possible assets.

security.title: Amazon Macie
security.question: Sensitive data discovery
security.copy: Discover/classify supported sensitive content in eligible S3 general purpose buckets.
security.caveat: Findings do not themselves redact data; unsupported objects need another path.

security.title: AWS Security Hub
security.question: Findings aggregation and prioritization
security.copy: Centralize, correlate and prioritize supported findings; Security Hub CSPM includes posture checks and service integrations.
security.caveat: Use supported integrations. Findings need triage and remediation; raw CloudTrail logs are not automatically findings.

security.title: AWS AppConfig
security.question: Application configuration deployment
security.copy: Validate and deploy configuration/feature flags through controlled rollouts; apps retrieve them through supported agents/APIs.
security.caveat: Separate from resource security auditing. The application must read and apply deployed values.

query.title: Rank / context
query.detail: Rerank and prune within token budget
